title: Bleachers' Jack Antonoff Declares 'This Version of Modernity Is Trash' on New Album
summary:
Imagine a world where, despite all our arguments, we all secretly agree on one thing: the way we live now is kind of terrible. That's the provocative thesis behind *everyone for ten minutes*, the latest album from Jack Antonoff's band Bleachers.

Antonoff, known for producing Taylor Swift and Lorde, told NPR he rarely writes from a universal perspective. But this time, he felt compelled. "We've never disagreed more. We've never been more torn apart," he said. "And yet there's one core thing that everyone agrees on, which is: this version of modernity is trash. No one's having a good time."

He sees evidence of this collective discontent in a cultural shift: people are flocking to movie theaters, collecting vinyl records, and attending concerts in droves. It's a nostalgia for a more analog, tangible world—a craving for connection that screens can't satisfy.

Antonoff's own journey began in cramped bars. In the song "the van," he recalls touring with early bands, playing to just nine people. "If you can find joy playing to nine people in a bar, that never leaves you," he said. That ethos now fuels his stadium shows, where he tries to honor each fan as an individual.

Grief is another cornerstone of the album. Antonoff's sister died when he was 18, and he describes a culture that is "death-closeted"—unwilling to talk openly about loss. "I went through years obsessing about it," he said. "It's baked into the work I do because I really got going in the years when I was dealing with the most grief."

Yet the album also celebrates love. Antonoff married actress Margaret Qualley in 2023, and "dirty wedding dress" captures the bubble of intimacy they felt inside the venue, oblivious to outside crowds. He cites a psychological study suggesting our brains can only truly empathize with about 125 people. "I think it's beautiful," he said. "We have our capacity. My partner, my band, my family, my audience—this is who is allowed in."

Ultimately, Antonoff sees Bleachers as a sanctuary. "Bleachers is for anybody, not everybody," he said. It's an invitation to find joy in the small, real moments—even when modernity feels like trash.
why_it_matters: In a world where teenagers spend hours on social media but report rising loneliness, Antonoff’s message reminds us that genuine connection—to music, to friends, to community—can’t be replaced by screens. Understanding the grief that underlies his songs might also help young people talk more openly about loss instead of hiding it.

background_read: Jack Antonoff, the frontman of Bleachers, is also a Grammy-winning record producer who helped craft blockbuster albums for Taylor Swift ("1989") and Lorde (the stage name of New Zealand singer Ella Yelich-O'Connor, known for "Royals").

His claim that "this version of modernity is trash" lands at a time when Americans are buying vinyl records in record numbers—sales surpassed CDs in 2022 for the first time since the 1980s—and filling concert arenas, suggesting a broad cultural hunger for tangibility.

The figure "about 125 people" echoes a concept from evolutionary psychology: the British anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed that the human neocortex limits the number of meaningful relationships we can sustain to around 150.

Antonoff's sister died when he was 18 from cancer, a loss that has informed his music for years; many artists, from classical composers to modern rockers, have turned personal tragedy into lasting art.
NPR (National Public Radio), the outlet that aired his interview, is a listener-supported nonprofit known for in-depth cultural journalism.
Article_Structure: LEAD: The provocative thesis that everyone secretly agrees modernity is trash.
└─ SOURCE: Jack Antonoff of Bleachers, in an NPR interview.
MAIN ARGUMENT: Despite divisions, a universal discontent exists.
├─ EVIDENCE: People flocking to movie theaters, vinyl, concerts—a nostalgia for analog life.
├─ EARLY DAYS: Playing to nine people in bars taught him to find joy in small crowds.
└─ STADIUM ETHOS: He now tries to honor each fan individually.
├─ LOSS: His sister's death at 18 made him obsess—he critiques 'death-closeted' culture.
├─ LOVE: Marriage to Margaret Qualley in 2023 inspired 'dirty wedding dress' about intimacy.
└─ CAPACITY: Cites study that we can empathize with only ~125 people.
RESOLUTION: 'Bleachers is for anybody, not everybody'—a sanctuary for those who seek real moments.

perspectives.description: Antonoff’s perspective offers hope: admitting modern life feels "trash" can unite us and push us toward more authentic experiences, like live shows and tangible art. It encourages finding joy in small, real interactions rather than in digital metrics.

Some might argue he’s oversimplifying—modernity also brings medical advances, instant communication, and opportunities. Dismissing it all as "trash" ignores those benefits and could fuel a backwards-looking nostalgia that doesn’t solve real problems.

His "125 people" idea reflects a well-known psychological limit; anthropology shows that human communities often function best in small, tight-knit groups. The article thus highlights a tussle between our evolution and the hyperconnected global society we’ve built.

What if artists like Antonoff can reshape culture? By blending raw grief, analog warmth, and intimate performances, he might pioneer a new wave of music that values depth over spectacle, inspiring future generations to seek meaning beyond digital noise.
